video_title: Why China Is Going After Anthropic
gist: Former NSC China director Julian Gewirtz explains why Beijing has singled out Anthropic as emblematic of US AI hegemony, argues China's AI policy is driven by regime security and US cyber advances (Mythos), and details compute constraints (limited Nvidia buying, Huawei push, remote access via Malaysia), an emerging Chinese open-weight risk discourse, and why US–China AI cooperation must proceed incrementally from parallel self-interest.

themes.theme: Beijing's campaign against Anthropic and US AI firms

insights.claim: Beijing has attacked Anthropic in official state media more repeatedly and directly than almost any other American company in US–China history, including a commentary headlined 'Anthropic has contracted the American disease' ahead of Xi Jinping's US visit.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Anthropic carries elevated China political/regulatory risk and is a lightning rod in US–China tech rhetoric.
insights.quote: the headline was “Anthropic has contracted the American disease.”

insights.claim: Beijing treats all US AI labs as one monolithic project of American technological hegemony — calling Anthropic 'a monster bred by the American path' — so inter-lab differences in views matter little to China.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Differentiated China messaging by any single US lab is unlikely to buy it distinct treatment in Beijing.
insights.quote: Beijing said Anthropic is literally “a monster bred by the American path”

insights.claim: Messaging by any single CEO, including Dario Amodei, is unlikely to change Beijing's view; the biggest levers on China's AI safety stance are its own domestic risk perception, followed by the US making a 'costly signal' by actually regulating AI.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Watch Chinese domestic risk discourse and US regulation, not lab comms, as drivers of any US–China AI safety thaw.
insights.quote: My own strong view is that the most important thing that could cause Beijing to shift its current approach to AI safety is their own domestic sense of the risks.

insights.claim: US rhetoric of total AI 'primacy' or permanent dominance is the least helpful language for winning Chinese cooperation, as distinct from simply wanting a lead.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Policy rhetoric framing (lead vs. supremacy) shapes the feasibility of bilateral AI deals.

insights.claim: China's state media explicitly linked Anthropic's distillation report with Dario's call to 'pace the frontier' as one coordinated effort to make Chinese AI look bad and keep the US number one — a connection few Americans drew.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: China reads disparate US corporate actions as coordinated strategy; expect retaliation narratives to bundle them.
insights.quote: they connect dots in our system that we may not connect ourselves

insights.claim: Beijing's official line on distillation of American models is not denial but that it is normal practice which the US is twisting into something it is not.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Distillation-based IP disputes are unlikely to be resolved through Chinese concessions.

themes.theme: Chinese AI labs, data leaks and the state

insights.claim: Anthropic reported that user requests to Kimi (Moonshot) and DeepSeek models were being rerouted to Claude, including in one instance requests from a PLA official, exposing sensitive Chinese data.
insights.speaker: Tom Reed
insights.so_what: Chinese labs' reliance on US models creates security and embarrassment risk that may trigger state crackdowns on such dependence.
insights.quote: requests from users to Kimi models or models from DeepSeek were being rerouted to Claude

insights.claim: The Claude rerouting episode reflects how breakneck Chinese catch-up efforts have produced sloppiness and dependence on American models that is deeply embarrassing to Beijing; the CCP conversations with Moonshot and DeepSeek CEOs were likely as political as technical.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Expect tighter state oversight of Chinese labs' use of foreign models.

insights.claim: In China, a Hugging Face-style AI security incident would be treated first as a cybersecurity and regime-security issue, with incentives at every layer against disclosure — the public might never learn of it, and a METR-style third-party report would be highly unlikely.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Information asymmetry: Chinese AI incidents will be underreported, so absence of news is not evidence of safety.
insights.quote: at every layer, the incentives in that system are not to disclose more information, and certainly not to disclose it publicly

insights.claim: A major AI incident in China could trigger a 'broader rectification campaign' bringing the sector under greater central control, likely without public disclosure.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Tail risk of sudden regulatory crackdown on Chinese AI firms, analogous to past tech rectifications.

insights.claim: Some American labs have a track record of disclosing incidents and occasionally constraining their own racing — a very low bar that Chinese labs have not cleared — giving the US labs an edge on safety credibility despite a US government that does not seem responsible.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Lab-level asymmetry in transparency favors US labs in safety-sensitive procurement and policy debates.
insights.quote: very low bar, not a bar that the Chinese labs have cleared

insights.claim: Chinese lab staff interpreted the US lab employees' pacing letter cynically: 'The United States has been pacing the frontier for China for years' and they do not believe the US will slow down.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: US voluntary pacing proposals are unlikely to elicit reciprocal Chinese restraint.
insights.quote: The United States has been pacing the frontier for China for years.

insights.claim: Many Chinese AI labs are 'AGI-pilled' while the Chinese government has been much less so, though that is changing; the views shaping the CCP are increasingly internal reports rather than public essays, and differ from what DeepSeek CEO Liang Wenfeng might say on an investor call.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Lab rhetoric is a poor proxy for state intentions; focus on internal policy signals.
insights.quote: many of the labs are. The Chinese government has been much less oriented that way, but I think even that is changing

insights.claim: Chinese AI lab employees complain constantly about government overreach; their key asks include compute, capital, and relief from new rules barring model-company employees and even family members from traveling abroad without permission.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Exit restrictions hamper talent recruitment (e.g., PRC nationals in the US weighing return offers), a drag on Chinese labs.

insights.claim: Chinese regulators blocked Meta's near-complete acquisition of Manus, a buzzy Chinese startup that had moved to Singapore — a founder's nightmare signaling that Beijing can kill cross-border exits.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Chinese-origin AI startups carry exit/M&A risk even after redomiciling abroad; discounts for acquirers and VCs.
insights.quote: the Chinese regulators came and yanked the chain and shut it down

themes.theme: Compute, chips and leading indicators of Chinese AGI belief

insights.claim: Beijing remains significantly constrained on compute and sees itself as behind; Gewirtz thinks it unlikely China becomes much less compute-constrained.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Compute scarcity remains China's binding constraint; supports demand for chips via any available channel.
insights.quote: right now Beijing is still significantly constrained on compute

insights.claim: Despite the Trump administration approving sales of previously restricted Nvidia chips, Beijing is buying them in limited quantities because Xi wants domestic compute reliance (especially Huawei) and Chinese firms can access top compute remotely in third-country data centres such as Malaysia, plus smuggling.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Approved China sales may underwhelm for Nvidia; Huawei benefits from policy-driven substitution; Malaysian data centres are a channel.
insights.quote: Beijing is buying them in quite limited quantities

insights.claim: Ding Xuexiang, a top Xi adviser coordinating compute and AI policy, reportedly told the sector that if forced to choose, go slower rather than depend on foreign compute — reportedly calling buyers of non-domestic chips traitors.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Political pressure caps Chinese demand for US chips regardless of US export policy.
insights.quote: if there’s a tradeoff between going a little bit slower and making sure that you’re not dependent on foreign compute, go a little bit slower

insights.claim: The best leading indicators that Beijing believes in imminent transformative AI/RSI would be material moves — centralising compute and aggressively buying American chips — rather than speeches from leaders like Wang Huning or He Lifeng.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Track Chinese compute centralisation and Nvidia import volumes as a signal of Beijing's AGI conviction.
insights.quote: you’d see them centralise compute, you’d see them more aggressively buy American chips

insights.claim: China's AI policy, dubbed 'AI Plus', aims to integrate AI into everything — manufacturing, robotics, the military and the state security apparatus — diffusing responsibility across government.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Chinese AI adoption is diffusion-led into industry, supporting embodied AI and robotics demand.

insights.claim: China's ageing population drives hopes that automation, robotics and embodied AI will let it maintain or increase manufacturing dominance as cheap-labour advantages fade.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for Chinese robotics/automation investment.

insights.claim: Gewirtz guesses that, if pressed, Chinese leaders would say the US is in an AI bubble with a lot of speculation, viewing American capitalism as irrational.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Beijing may read US AI valuations as fragile, shaping its strategic patience.
insights.quote: they would say there’s an AI bubble, there’s a lot of speculation

themes.theme: CCP risk perception: regime security, Mythos and open weights

insights.claim: The CCP's top AI concern is regime security and political/social stability; when Chinese discourse says 'loss of control' it means loss of political control as well as loss of human control over AI.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: AI incidents threatening information control are the ones most likely to change Chinese AI policy.
insights.quote: they don’t simply mean it in the way that a lot of AI safety folks here mean it

insights.claim: Anthropic's Mythos and the sense that the US is gaining extraordinary cyber capabilities was the most significant event shaping Beijing's AI-risk thinking over the past year, with the US now a close second threat after loss of political control.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: US frontier cyber capabilities are driving Chinese counter-responses and securitisation of AI.
insights.quote: the most significant event in shaping the evolution of Beijing’s thinking about AI risks over the course of the past year or so is Mythos

insights.claim: An AI-assisted, responsibly disclosed vulnerability in Tencent's WeChat was patched, but how the government processed it never became public.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: AI-found vulnerabilities in core Chinese platforms are a live regime-security issue.
insights.quote: “We patched the vulnerability.”

insights.claim: A new Chinese discourse is emerging on the risks of open-weight models: the TC260 3.0 AI safety governance framework warns that open-source releases lower barriers to sophisticated cyberattacks, and scholars now argue 'we can't have unrestricted openness'.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Possible future tightening of Chinese open-weight releases would change competitive dynamics for global open models.
insights.quote: open-source releases lowering the barriers to conducting sophisticated cyberattacks

insights.claim: China's open-weight strategy serves to undercut American companies, spread Chinese influence and do so on a limited compute budget, while feeding a 'China stands for openness' narrative; Beijing only needs to be more open than the US, giving it room to restrict.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Chinese open models pressure US pricing; Beijing can pivot quickly if security risks rise.
insights.quote: They just need to be more so-called “open” than the United States is

insights.claim: Xi Jinping left the door open to updating AI policy at the World AI Conference, invoking flexibility — an unusual signal — and Gewirtz expects China's own perception of AI risk to evolve, possibly sooner than expected.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Chinese AI policy shifts may come abruptly; monitor domestic risk discourse.
insights.quote: I think it could happen sooner than many of us expect

insights.claim: Xi Jinping positions technology as 'the main battlefield of international competition' and a physical instantiation of political power; after missing the Industrial Revolution, China intends to lead this revolution.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: China will not voluntarily cede AI leadership; expect sustained state investment.
insights.quote: the main battlefield of international competition

insights.claim: The likeliest route to Xi taking explosive AI progress seriously is seeing the US pull ahead quickly while it does not feel like it is happening in China, which could produce divergent paths including a small chance Beijing concludes pacing is in its interest.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: US breakthroughs could raise both escalation and deal probabilities.
insights.quote: Small probability, but nonzero.

insights.claim: Gewirtz had low expectations for the Bessent–He Lifeng and Trump–Xi meetings on AI and they were not met: no technical working group and no crisis-communication cadence, only a vague verbal commitment to call each other.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: No institutional US–China AI channel exists; incident escalation risk remains.
insights.quote: pretty low expectations, and they were not met

insights.claim: The US–China relationship is 'K-shaped': an upward leg of leader-level warmth and optics, and a lower leg of continuing military, technological and economic competition; China sees Trump's warmth as little more than buying time.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Summit optics overstate stability; underlying competition and policy reversal risk persist.
insights.quote: I’ve described the kind of current state of the US–China relationship as K-shaped

insights.claim: Gewirtz's biggest day-to-day worries for US–China relations are unpredictable leader-level interactions (Trump changing his mind) and accident risk from militaries operating in close proximity in the Western Pacific.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Headline risk from summit breakdowns or military incidents.

insights.claim: A marked deterioration of US–China relations, back to 'Trump in 2020', would further intensify China's zero-sum, national-security frame for AI.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Trade-war relapse would harden Chinese AI securitisation.

insights.claim: The first sticking point in US CAISI–China technical cooperation would be terminology: in Chinese, safety and security are the same word, anquan, confusing non-English-speaking experts.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Track II dialogues and shared vocabulary are prerequisites for any AI agreement.
insights.quote: in Chinese, safety and security are the same word, anquan

insights.claim: The deal most appealing to the CCP would be unilateral US restraint; constraints on China's own development are unappealing, creating a prisoner's-dilemma dynamic, while verification science must catch up to the frontier.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Bilateral AI pauses are improbable near-term; verification tech (compute, energy, data-centre monitoring) is a precondition.
insights.quote: the most appealing thing would be unilateral restraint from the United States

insights.claim: Verification of any AI pause would need robust technical means — size of training runs, data-centre locations, energy use, capability testing — since trust is low and espionage alone is insufficient.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Demand for compute-governance and verification technology could grow if agreements emerge.

insights.claim: Gewirtz and Matt Sheehan advocate building from parallel self-interested actions — e.g., neither side wants loss of control or proliferation to bad actors — as building blocks for later ambition, with incremental 'crossing the river by feeling for the stones' rather than grand-bargain design.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Expect incremental, parallel national regulation rather than a sweeping treaty.
insights.quote: crossing the river by feeling for the stones

insights.claim: US bargaining leverage rests on Chris McGuire's 'three-legged stool' — domestic regulation as costly signals, export controls that could be tightened, and bilateral/global diplomacy — plus broader leverage such as fixing rare-earths dependency.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Export-control tightening and rare-earth indigenisation remain live US policy levers.
insights.quote: you’ve got kind of a three-legged stool

insights.claim: Beijing has some domestic AI regulation (deepfake/AI content labelling, chatbot rules for minors) yet the US still fears it catching up, undermining the claim that any regulation loses the race.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Domestic AI regulation need not cost competitive position; distinct from pacing.
insights.quote: there’s a bit of a fallacy embedded in the idea that any AI regulation is at odds

insights.claim: China believes the US misjudges fundamental risks — citing the 2008 financial crisis and Bill Clinton's 'nailing Jell-O to the wall' prediction about internet control, which China proved wrong.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Beijing discounts US risk warnings, including on AI.
insights.quote: We are going to nail Jell-O to the wall

themes.theme: Taiwan, Global South and information influence

insights.claim: For Beijing, Taiwan is a longstanding regime priority not driven by AI; TSMC's centrality is secondary, and the idea China would invade because the US neared RSI should not drive analysis, though it can't be fully dismissed.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Taiwan risk pricing should hinge on politics, not AI timelines.
insights.quote: For Beijing, Taiwan is not about AI, right?

insights.claim: Beijing hopes Taiwan's January 2028 presidential election favours the KMT, making the political path feel more open than in a long time; the approach is sustained coercion while avoiding costly military options.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Near-term invasion risk appears lower ahead of the 2028 election; watch KMT nominee.
insights.quote: Taiwan has a presidential election in January 2028

insights.claim: Polling shows the US at the very bottom of rankings for optimism about AI benefits and China at the very top, reflected in seamless everyday AI use like real-time translation.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Consumer AI adoption headwinds in the US versus tailwinds in China.
insights.quote: the United States is at the very bottom of rankings for optimism about the benefits of AI for people, and China is at the very top

insights.claim: Chinese discourse increasingly sees shaping training corpora as an opportunity to influence international narratives (e.g., on Taiwan), and models give different answers in Chinese vs. English.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Model provenance and training data become geopolitical risk factors for AI buyers.

insights.claim: ChatGPT appears to have greater facility with the Chinese internet (e.g., finding WeChat links) than Claude, per both Gewirtz and Reed.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Minor product differentiation in China-focused research use.
insights.quote: ChatGPT somehow has seemingly greater facility with the Chinese parts of the internet than Claude

insights.claim: China's Global South strategy is visible across varied sites: India pushing back by blocking Chinese apps, Central Asia's China–Russia competition, Egypt upgrading China ties, Mexico's scale-up of Chinese manufacturing, Peru's Chinese-built Pacific megaport, and Africa.
insights.speaker: Julian Gewirtz
insights.so_what: Chinese manufacturing relocation to Mexico and port infrastructure like Peru's are key geoeconomic shifts.
insights.quote: Peru, where China has been building this megaport on the Pacific coast
